HISTORY OF SAN JOSE AREA
Citywide
On June 3, 1777, Don Felipe Neve, the third Spanish Governor of California, suggested to the central government of Mexico the establishment of three settlements in Alta California for the purpose of serving as food production centers for the Spanish missions and garrisons of the region. One of the settlements recommended was to be located on the Rio de Guadalupe seventy-eight miles from Monterey, forty-eight miles from the San Francisco Presidio, and two and a quarter miles from Mission Santa Clara. Here, on November 29, 1777, nine soldiers, a cowboy servant, and fifty-eight settlers under the leadership of Lieutenant-Commander Jose Joaquin Moraga founded El Pueblo de San Jose de Guadalupe (Gudde 1969, Sawyer 1922).
Each settler coming to San Jose received a plot of ground for cultivation and a ten dollar per month stipend. In addition, heads of families were given on loan two cows, two oxen, two mares, two beeves, two sheep, two goats, and one mule (Winther 1935).
In 1797 the pueblo was moved to less than a mile south of the city's present center because of flooding in the lower marshy location. The population of the pueblo increased to 170 by the end of the century and by 1820 numbered 240. The number of houses in San Jose was reported to be 20 in 1814. This number had scarcely doubled by 1835 (Sawyer 1922).
Americans began to immigrate in large numbers to the Santa Clara Valley after 1844 and by 1847 there were more than 100 living in or near San Jose. A hotel had been established by one American, Zachariah Jones, and others had begun a livery stable and a number of stores.
